title: What would you say are the most common tropes in RPG Maker games that give it a bad rap?

The Cookie/Cut style.
People quite often say that once you play one, you've played them all.
And one thing I noticed is that the combat in some games is not beginner-friendly.

As the dev, you know the enemies and how your combat works, but for new players who are still learning might find starting fights hard due to them still learning the game.

Nothing in the makers is automatically bad by default.
the problem is that no matter what else, making a good game is WORK - a lot of work.
and there were too many people that barely understood the maker and made a quick 'pseudo-game' in a weekend, trying to sell it for quick cash.
that never works, but it results in the already mentioned shovelware, and at one time in the past (before they charged for game admission) that Steam was flooded with RM-shovelware.
most of the bad bias came from that, and the RPG-Makers have been slowly clawing themselves out of that bottom pit ever since Valve installed some quality control and the payment requirement to the games they admit.

posts.author: Solarae
posts.body:
I’m new to RPG Maker MV, so I’ve been slowly adding non-default assets (NPCs, enemies, battlebacks, etc.). I actually do like the built-in tilesets, though. I just didn’t like how clean they looked, so I pixelated them like in the second image to better match the style I’m going for.
I’m working on this game solo and planning it over the course of a year, so creating everything from scratch is pretty challenging. That said, I’ve been collaborating with an artist for some sprites, and they’ve been doing amazing work. I’m also actively looking for assets outside of the default RPG Maker MV ones whenever possible.
For the story, I’ve had a few people playtest it because I know that what makes sense to me might not be clear to new players. They might get confused, spot plot holes, or just not find it engaging overall.
My biggest issue is something others have also pointed out: the use of default assets. I’ve also been told that many people don’t want to play an indie game unless it fully uses its own original assets first of all. Realistically, for me to achieve that level, I would need a bigger budget and a team. Unfortunately, I don’t have the funds or team members, and I can’t afford to pay people large amounts. On top of that, I’m not even sure if the game will take off in a big way, being just a new solo dev to RPG Maker, so I have to be careful with what I can realistically build.
While I am still using the tilesets (pixeled), I’m trying to replace everything else I can so the game doesn’t end up feeling like it’s built entirely from default resources. I will also add that the base music isn't great, so I'm trying to replace all of that as well. (Also, As I have been working, hearing more and more of the base music in videos, it doesn't sound unique anymore.)
Also, I really like the character creator for the faces. It gets pretty close to what I want for showing the characters’ expressions. I’d honestly love to hire artists to refine them, but right now, as a solo developer with no budget beyond my own pocket money, the RPG Maker MV character creator is what I’m limited to.

posts.author: Gamera
posts.body:
I play the more adventure & exploration game style RPG Maker stuff.  I'd say for those, bad writing.  That's a very, very big field, but it's hard to name all the common or bad things in titles like that.  Here's a few thoughts:
Spoiler:
Small List of Common Problems
1. Multiple endings for the sake of multiple endings - I think less games go for this nowadays, but if you want to have multiple endings, you might as well make them meaningful or reveal something to the story.  Pulling stuff out of nowhere is jarring and usually ends up padding replays instead of rewarding the player for making different choices.
2. Weird Pacing - There's clear points of some games where the creator wanted to rush through from a plot point they don't care about to something they really want to write.  Sometimes there's clear spots that the creator did not know how to transition from one point to another, or ran out of time/damns to finish certain areas.  The whiplash can be bad, and it doesn't help that it isn't easy to learn.
3. Repetition - This is something more acceptable for Japanese translated games (to a point): repeating what someone else just said is common in speech.  Those who make English-first games need to cut down on repetition, whether it is repeating sentences in different ways or describing a brown fuzzy teddy bear as "a brown fuzzy teddy bear" (thank you, I can see that).  Adding extra information like how the bear smells like chocolate or how it seems to be well cared for gives more character to flavor text.
4.  Padding - It's ok to have a short game.  Content > Filler.  Sometimes, people want to write to a specific word count to give more content to people.  But if the content is clearly there to waste time, the overall experience is dulled by the filler.
5. Nothing to Find/Interact With - If your game is based on exploration, please make sure to have something interesting happen if you click on things.  The size of the map, the more things should be interactable.  Opening cabinets, rolling boulders, and other minor things can help make a world more lively.
SolaraeStudio said:
My biggest issue is something others have also pointed out: the use of default assets. I’ve also been told that many people don’t want to play an indie game unless it fully uses its own original assets first of all.
Click to expand...
It's one of those things that bites, but is what it is.  Even games with original graphics can underperform if they're not particularly interesting in plot or gameplay.  I think cutting your teeth on small games with default graphics can help build a fanbase that can help connect you with people who can make graphics & help fund projects, but that also isn't a guarentee.
Honestly, I think people will take a look at your game if you use pre-made assets as long as your map design looks like thought was put into it.
Candacis
' old blog has some nice examples of maps using default assets.
This guy on Devianart
did some nice maps with premade assets.  Things like
A small town interior looks more interesting when not in a complete square grid & good use of space (Candacis):
Or this one
by RPG_Girl8, just a decent use of overall space with decent details and a nice layout.
The
Mapping thread
(and the previous 11 threads!) have some great examples. Adding things like lighting, elevation, and points of interest helps a ton.  Your favorite RPGs (or 3/4ths view games like 2D Zelda) are also a good idea to look at for map layouts.  Even games with original graphics have a problem with managing space, light, & interest.
As long as you don't half butt the maps, you can probably get some decent interest.  There will always be people who decide to dive into every single RPG Maker game regardless of quality... just because. So at least that helps a bit. ;w;

Yeah, I’ve definitely worried about the default assets. I’ve seen people say they won’t even try a game if it uses them, which got in my head a bit. But I started my project using them while building the world, and honestly, I think they can work if the map design and overall presentation feel intentional.
I agree a lot with what you said, especially about pacing and padding. I’m trying to focus on building the world’s logic first, then the story inside it, so things don’t feel rushed or disconnected. I also want to make sure exploration actually feels rewarding, with quests, both small and large, that let players interact with NPCs, build relationships, and have some kind of impact on the world.
As a solo dev, it is a bit overwhelming, and I worry about missing things like pacing issues or filler. I also really want to avoid making my characters feel like a “Mary Sue” situation. I’d rather they struggle and leave room for interpretation, like whether they’re processing grief, in denial, or actually moving on, so the player can read into it themselves.
and yeah, I get what you mean about repetition too, I’ve been trying to be more mindful about not over explaining things and instead adding details that actually build atmosphere or character.
I think you’re right, strong writing, good pacing, and meaningful interaction matter way more than whether the assets are default or custom.

The writing will be fine as long as you just ask for outside opinions every once in a while like you're doing.  You're aware of possible problems, you don't have to be too anxious that you'll fall into the trap.
For a Mary Sue in particular is less a character and more of a type of story: Mary Sue comes into a story and sucks all the meaningful conflict out by making every solution simple and easy, focusing entirely on that character's melodrama (and not actual conflict) to the detriment of other characters, and usually centers around the main character's/author's feelings and ego as absolute morality.  All meaningful conflict is sucked out, and situtations that either create specific melodrama the creator wants (usually showing how awesome, desirable, pitiful, or powerful the character is).  Mary Sues of any gender happen when people forget that characters taking their time to grow and overcome obstacles.  From the way you talked, I think you'll be fine.
The other thing you should remember is that many people have many different tastes.  Something that you enjoy in a story can be a turn off for someone else.  This isn't a bad thing: you have your likes and dislikes too.  Sometimes when you ask for others opinions, you can tell they just personally are not a fan of something - and that's fine.  That means you can still write it anyways because you're a fan of it, and there's likely several more people like you who enjoy it.  This can be anything from redemption arcs to talks about sandwiches to pep talk speeches - you can enjoy writing what you like and not always worry about others either.   Most of the time when you make a game, people will enjoy the story as long as there's effort put in and it doesn't detract from the gameplay.

At least you'd be working on your game even if it filled with RTP. You can go back to replacing it later. And if it still stays RTP, at least you can say you made something.
